{{Short description|Scale level in statistics}}
{{Confusing|date=July 2025}}

There is no single definition of an '''absolute scale'''. In statistics and measurement theory, it is simply a ratio scale in which the unit of measurement is fixed, and values are obtained by counting.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Absolute scale |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095344949 |work=Oxford Reference }}</ref> Another definition tells us it is the count of the elements in a set, with its natural origin being zero, the empty set.{{fact|date=August 2025}} Some sources tell us that even time can be measured in an absolute scale, proving year zero is measured from the beginning of the universe.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Absolute vs Relative Scales|url=https://www.westfield.ma.edu/PersonalPages/cmasi/gen_chem1/Temperature%20page/abs%20vs%20rel%20scale%20folder/absolute_vs_relative_scale.htm|access-date=2021-10-03|website=www.westfield.ma.edu}}{{self-published inline|date=August 2025}}</ref> Colloquially, the [[Kelvin temperature scale]], where absolute zero is the temperature at which molecular energy is at a minimum, and the [[Rankine temperature scale]] are also referred to as absolute scales. In that case, an absolute scale is a system of [[measurement]] that begins at a minimum, or zero point, and progresses in only one direction.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Absolute Scale definition {{!}} Psychology Glossary {{!}} alleydog.com|url=https://www.alleydog.com/glossary/definition.php?term=Absolute+Scale|access-date=2021-10-03|website=www.alleydog.com}}{{rs|date=August 2025}}</ref>

==Features==
{{Empty section|date=July 2025}}

==Uses==
Absolute scales are used when precise values are needed in comparison to a natural, unchanging zero point. Measurements of [[length]], [[area (mathematics)|area]] and [[volume]] are inherently absolute, although measurements of distance are often based on an arbitrary starting point. Measurements of [[weight]] can be absolute, such as [[atomic weight]], but more often they are measurements of the relationship between two [[mass]]es, while measurements of [[speed]] are relative to an arbitrary [[frame of reference|reference frame]]. (Unlike many other measurements without a known, absolute minimum, speed has a known maximum and can be measured from a purely relative scale.) Absolute scales can be used for measuring a variety of things, from the flatness of an [[optical flat]] to neuroscientific tests.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berka |first1=Karel |title=Measurement |chapter=Scales |series=Boston Studies in the Philosophy of Science |date=1983 |volume=72 |pages=83–100 |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-7828-7_4 |isbn=978-94-009-7830-0 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Russell |first1=Elbert W. |title=The Scientific Foundation of Neuropsychological Assessment |chapter=Brain-Function Analysis |date=2012 |pages=69–110 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-416029-3.00004-X |isbn=978-0-12-416029-3 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Balmer |first1=Robert T. |title=Modern Engineering Thermodynamics |chapter=Thermodynamic Properties |date=2011 |pages=57–98 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-374996-3.00003-8 |isbn=978-0-12-374996-3 }}</ref>
